examples.problem_statement: x, y, and z are integers, xyz \ge 0, yz < 0, and y < 0. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: z. Choose whether Quantity A is greater, Quantity B is greater, the two quantities are equal, or the relationship cannot be determined.

solution.description: Combine the two given facts about y and z: a negative product with a negative first factor forces the second factor to be positive, so z is positive.
Treat yz as a single negative factor; for x times a negative quantity to be non-negative, x itself must be negative or zero.
Substitute the bounds just derived into the two quantities: Quantity A is at most 0 while Quantity B is strictly positive.
Compare the bounds; since the largest A can be is 0 and B is always above 0, Quantity B is greater in every case.

key_reminders: A product of two numbers is negative only when the two factors have opposite signs.
If a product of three integers is non-negative and two of them multiply to a negative, the third must be negative or zero.
In quantitative comparison, a conclusion holds only if it holds for every value allowed by the constraints.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that x = 0 is allowed by xyz \ge 0, and then wrongly treating x as strictly negative.
Reading yz < 0 with y < 0 as forcing z negative instead of positive.

concept.sub_category: table-based data interpretation with percentages and ratios

examples.problem_statement: Study the table of the number of boys of standard XI participating in different games (class XI D column: Chess 4, Badminton 12, Table Tennis 8, Hockey 4, Football 12, Total No. of Boys 40). Every student of each class of standard XI participates in exactly one game, and in each class the number of girls participating in each game is 25% of the number of boys participating in that game. All the boys of class XI D passed the annual examination but a few girls failed. If all the boys and girls who passed and entered XII D are in the ratio of boys to girls as 5:1, what would be the number of girls who failed in class XI D?

solution.description: Read the total number of boys in class XI D straight from the last row of the table's XI D column.
Apply the note that girls number 25% of the boys to get the total number of girls in class XI D.
Carry the boys forward unchanged, because the question states every boy of XI D passed and moved into XII D.
Use the 5:1 boys-to-girls ratio in XII D to convert the 40 boys into the matching number of girls who passed.
Subtract the girls who passed from the girls originally in XI D to find how many girls failed.

key_reminders: Girls in any class or game equal 25% of the corresponding number of boys.
A boys-to-girls ratio of 5:1 means the number of girls is the number of boys divided by 5.
Students who failed are the difference between the original class strength and those who entered the next class.
common_mistakes: Using a games-row figure from the XI D column (such as 12) instead of the class total of 40.
Multiplying 40 by 5 instead of dividing when applying the 5:1 ratio.

concept.sub_category: ordering games with conditional entry rules

examples.problem_statement: The six messages on an answering machine were each left by one of Fleure, Greta, Hildy, Liam, Pasquale, or Theodore, consistent with the following: At most one person left more than one message. No person left more than three messages. If the first message is Hildy's, the last is Pasquale's. If Greta left any message, Fleure and Pasquale did also. If Fleure left any message, Pasquale and Theodore did also, all of Pasquale's preceding any of Theodore's. If Pasquale left any message, Hildy and Liam did also, all of Hildy's preceding any of Liam's. The first and last messages on the answering machine could be the first and second messages left by which one of the following? (A) Fleure (B) Hildy (C) Liam (D) Pasquale (E) Theodore

solution.operation: Apply the rule 'if the first message is Hildy's, the last is Pasquale's' to answer choice (B).
solution.description: Rule out Hildy immediately: if Hildy is first, the last message must be Pasquale's, so Hildy cannot own both the first and the last message.

solution.operation: Read the stem: the named person leaves the first and last messages as their first and second messages.
solution.result: That person leaves exactly two messages, and four other people leave one each to reach six.
solution.description: Interpret the question stem rather than testing choices: since at most one person leaves more than one message and this person's second message is the last one, that person leaves exactly two, so four more distinct people are needed for the remaining four messages.

solution.operation: Fill the four remaining slots from the always-required P, T, H, L plus one more person.
solution.result: The fifth person must be Fleure.
solution.description: Determine who joins the doubler: P, T, H and L are always in, and choosing Greta would drag Fleure in as well, giving six people with no room for anyone to leave two messages, so Fleure is the fifth.

solution.operation: With F and P in, trigger 'all Pasquale's precede any Theodore's' and 'all Hildy's precede any Liam's'.
solution.result: P - T (all) and H - L (all) are active.
solution.description: Activate the ordering consequences of Fleure and Pasquale being present, which lock Pasquale entirely before Theodore and Hildy entirely before Liam.

solution.operation: Test P, T, H, L against those ordering blocks for holding both the first and last message.
solution.description: Eliminate the remaining ordered players: Pasquale could be first but a Theodore must follow every Pasquale so Pasquale cannot also be last, and Theodore cannot be first for the mirror reason, with Liam similarly blocked, leaving Fleure.

key_reminders: At most one person leaves more than one message, so the person holding the first and last message leaves exactly two.
Fleure's presence forces Pasquale and Theodore in with all Pasquale's messages before any of Theodore's.
Pasquale's presence forces Hildy and Liam in with all Hildy's messages before any of Liam's.
common_mistakes: Testing each answer choice by building full orderings instead of first deducing that exactly five people leave messages.
Overlooking that adding Greta forces Fleure in too, which would need six people and leave no one able to double up.
